b: While we have dozens of biomarkers that can help assess cardiovascular or metabolic health, our primary measure of the impact of aging on our risk of death and disease remains chronological age. It is therefore easy to understand the appeal of biological-aging clocks: a simple blood test that could quantify how quickly someone is aging might help individuals understand their health and give researchers a way to evaluate interventions intended to slow age-related decline.

But as we have discussed previously, the promise of these tests currently exceeds the evidence. Aging clocks are indirect estimates, not direct measurements of biological age, and their results can be affected by biological and technical variability. Their accuracy for any individual remains uncertain, and even if a clock performs reasonably well on average, that does not mean it will perform equally well for everyone. Most methylation clock studies do not report the ancestry, location, or other demographic information about the participants on whose data they are built. Before these tests can be used to compare individuals or guide research across populations, we need to know whether the underlying algorithms generalize beyond the populations represented in the data used to build them.

A recent study sought to determine whether DNA-methylation aging clocks work equally well across genetically diverse and admixed populations.1 The researchers analyzed blood methylation data from more than 600 participants in the MAGENTA cohort, approximately half of whom had Alzheimer’s disease and half of whom were matched controls. The cohort included African American, Cuban, White, Peruvian, and Puerto Rican participants. They also included three independent datasets comprising more than 2,500 people of African or European ancestry.

They applied several commonly used aging clocks, including the Horvath, Hannum, Zhang, PhenoAge, and DunedinPACE clocks. Each of these clocks was developed for somewhat different purposes, with the three first-generation clocks primarily estimating chronological age, PhenoAge estimating biological age and disease risk, and DunedinPACE estimating the rate of aging.
Age prediction was not equally accurate across ancestries

The researchers first assessed how well the Horvath clock could predict chronological age. A clock that perfectly tracked chronological age would have a correlation coefficient of 1, meaning that its estimates would align exactly with participants’ actual ages. When applied to the White participants in the MAGENTA cohort, the Horvath clock produced a correlation of 0.72—not perfect, but comparable to what has been reported in other studies of older adults.

But the results differed substantially across the other cohorts. The correlation was similar in the Cuban and Peruvian participants, at 0.68 and 0.72, respectively, but considerably lower among African American participants, at 0.51, and Puerto Rican participants, at 0.45. These were also the groups with the greatest proportions of African genetic ancestry, suggesting that clock performance worsened as African ancestry increased.

Correlation tells us how closely the estimates track actual age, while prediction error tells us how far off the estimates are in years. The median absolute error was 5.10 years in White controls, 5.38 years in African American controls, and 5.19 years in Puerto Rican controls.

This was not simply a problem with the Horvath clock. The other first-generation clocks—the Hannum and Zhang models—showed a similar pattern, with lower age-prediction accuracy in the groups with substantial African ancestry. The researchers also found the same general pattern when they tested independent datasets, suggesting a broader limitation in the portability of these clocks rather than a problem with one particular test.

Having established that the clocks were less accurate at estimating chronological age in some groups, the researchers next asked whether they could identify accelerated aging in people with Alzheimer’s disease.

For the clocks that were not designed to measure the pace of aging, the researchers derived age-acceleration estimates by determining whether a person’s methylation age was higher or lower than expected for their chronological age. DunedinPACE was evaluated separately because it was designed to estimate the pace of aging directly, rather than simply predict age.

Among White participants, those with Alzheimer’s generally had higher age-acceleration estimates than controls, although the differences were modest and reached statistical significance for only some clocks. The results were less consistent across the other ancestry-defined cohorts: No single clock consistently showed greater age acceleration in Alzheimer’s patients across all groups. In some cohorts, the controls even had numerically (though not necessarily statistically) higher age-acceleration estimates than the Alzheimer’s patients.

DunedinPACE performed better than the other clocks in this analysis. It identified a significantly greater pace of aging in the Alzheimer’s group among White, African American, and Puerto Rican participants—but not among Cuban or Peruvian participants. Thus, even in a disease strongly associated with aging, and even with a clock designed to assess rate of aging, these measures did not reliably identify who was aging faster across populations.
When ancestry-related methylation looks like aging

Clocks that work well for one group but poorly for another are not particularly useful as measures of the underlying aging process. Understanding why they fail to generalize, however, may help researchers design more reliable clocks in the future.

Most of these clocks assess methylation at specific locations in the DNA called CpG sites. DNA methylation involves attaching a small chemical group, called a methyl group, to the DNA. Patterns of methylation can change with age and disease, which is why they can be useful for estimating biological age. But methylation is also influenced by many other factors, including genetics, time of day, recent meals, stress levels, and the types of cells present in a blood sample.2,3 A methylation difference is therefore not automatically a signal of aging.

The researchers reasoned that ancestry-related differences in methylation could be one reason the clocks performed differently across populations. They first compared methylation across the genome in people of African and European ancestry and identified more than 70,000 CpG sites with significantly different methylation patterns. These differences may also reflect age, disease, or environmental exposures; the key issue is that a site that varies systematically with ancestry does not provide a clean or unambiguous signal of aging.

Because each clock uses only a small subset of the millions of CpG sites in the genome, the researchers then determined how many of these ancestry-associated sites were actually included in each clock.

Depending on the clock, between 7% and 25% of its CpG sites showed differences in methylation between the African- and European-ancestry groups. Moreover, the clocks that included a greater proportion of these ancestry-associated sites tended to show poorer performance across populations. This does not prove that these sites caused the prediction errors, but it supports the idea that ancestry-related methylation differences contributed to the clocks’ limited generalizability.

That overlap gave the researchers a reason to look more closely at whether genetic variants might contribute to prediction error. Some genetic variants, called methylation quantitative trait loci, or meQTLs, influence how much methylation occurs at a particular CpG site. They do not necessarily alter the CpG site itself; instead, they can affect the molecular machinery that regulates its methylation. In this study, meQTLs affecting clock-related CpG sites were more common among people with African genetic ancestry, making them a plausible contributor to the poorer performance of some clocks in these populations.

The Horvath clock showed one of the largest declines in performance across admixed populations, and it also contained the greatest proportion of CpG sites influenced by meQTLs. Of the 56 Horvath sites where methylation was associated with prediction error, 42 were linked to at least one meQTL. By contrast, DunedinPACE, which performed best at distinguishing Alzheimer’s cases from controls across the cohorts, contained no CpG sites with known meQTLs. This offers one possible explanation for its better portability.

It also suggests a potential strategy for developing more generalizable clocks: exclude CpG sites known to be influenced by common or ancestry-differentiated meQTLs. That is not a complete solution—DunedinPACE still did not perform equally well in every cohort—but it may reduce one source of ancestry-related prediction error.

Biological-age clocks are statistical models that use methylation patterns to estimate different aspects of aging, and their accuracy depends on how well those patterns represent the people to whom the clock is applied. A clock can perform well in the populations represented in its training data and still produce less reliable estimates in other groups—a problem that has also limited the generalizability of polygenic risk scores.

This does not mean that aging clocks have no value—it simply means that they require more rigorous validation before they can be used to make claims about an individual’s health or rate of aging. Future clocks will need to be developed and tested in more genetically diverse populations, with greater attention to the genetic and environmental factors that influence methylation.

For now, these epigenetic age scores cannot be used to reliably tell you whether you are aging more quickly or slowly than your chronological age suggests. Your score may reflect genuine biology, but it may also reflect technical noise, short-term factors such as a recent meal, or ancestry-associated methylation patterns that the clock cannot properly interpret. The promise of aging clocks is real. Realizing that promise will require knowing whether these tools are measuring aging—or simply reflecting how closely someone’s biology resembles the populations represented in the training data.
